title: Why knots hold
text: Knots are older than the wheel, older than the needle, quite possibly older than the plough, yet physics only {{1}} why they hold in 2023, when mathematicians finally published a {{2}} that predicts a knot's strength from its crossing structure. The everyday {{3}} is familiar to every sailor and climber: some knots slip, some jam, and the {{4}} between them is subtle — often a single extra twist. A knot's grip comes from {{5}}: as the rope is loaded, each curve presses against the next, and friction {{6}} the slip until it stops. That is why the same knot in slick fishing line fails where rough rope holds, and why the deadly mistake in joining two ropes is to pick knots that jam so hard they can never be untied. The 2023 work {{7}} a simple ratio — the number of twists per crossing — that lets engineers simulate rope behaviour without testing every knot to destruction. Sailors knew the answers for centuries. Now the equations finally {{8}} them.

'published a framework that predicts a knot's strength' — a systematic structure of theory; feedback = return information.
'the everyday observation is familiar' — what everyone has noticed; obstruction = a blockage.
'the contrast between them is subtle' — the difference; contempt = scorn.
'a knot's grip comes from friction' — the rubbing resistance of rope on rope; fission = splitting an atom.
'friction arrests the slip until it stops' — brings it to a halt; arraign = formally accuse in court.
'the work proposes a simple ratio' — puts it forward as an answer; suppose = assume without proof.
'the equations finally agree with them' — 'agree with' = give the same verdict; accept, adopt and admit do not form this pattern with 'with'.
